what: Build Check Part 1 (ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): every source the Source Register lists for a finding was reopened on 5 October 2026 and each recorded quotation looked for on its page.

checks.recorded: "Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes."
checks.page_wording: Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes.
checks.note: Word for word, under the bare-root heading of 'When to plant roses'; the page describes bare-root roses as lifted 'while dormant'. It supports the UK part only (nothing on New Zealand or Australia). The page gives two windows, not one continuous season, and the next sentence says 'Avoid planting in the middle of winter when the ground is frozen.'

checks.recorded: "Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes."
checks.page_wording: Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes.
checks.note: Word for word and about bare-root roses, so the RHS half of the finding is supported. This page says nothing about US practice, so the comparison rests on other sources. The RHS also says to avoid mid-winter when the ground is frozen.

checks.recorded: "Plant all year round, provided the ground is neither frozen, nor very dry."
checks.page_wording: Plant all year round, provided the ground is neither frozen, nor very dry.
checks.note: Word for word, under the 'containerised and container-grown roses' part of 'When to plant roses'. The two conditions (ground not frozen, not very dry) are the ones the finding refers to. UK source; no date shown.

checks.recorded: "Spacing depends on type and habit. Check catalogue or label details."
checks.page_wording: Spacing depends on type and habit. Check catalogue or label details.
checks.note: Word for word, in the planting steps. It supports only that spacing varies with the rose, and the page says 'type and habit', not 'mature size'. The page gives no distances at all, so it does not support the 50 cm to 1 m range.

checks.recorded: "as roses are at risk from replant disease."
checks.page_wording: ...exchange it with soil from a different part of the garden, as roses are at risk from replant disease, also known as soil sickness.
checks.note: The fragment is word for word and is about replacing old roses with new ones. It only names the risk; this page does not describe poor establishment or poor growth. The page's other name for it is 'soil sickness', not 'rose sickness'.

checks.recorded: "dig out the soil to a depth and width of 45cm (18in) and exchange it with soil from a different part of the garden"
checks.page_wording: If you are replacing old roses with new roses, ensure that you dig out the soil to a depth and width of 45cm (18in)...
checks.note: Word for word. It supports the 'replace the soil' remedy with one stated amount (45 cm deep and wide, swapped with soil from elsewhere in the garden). This page gives no other remedy: no planting elsewhere, no rotation, no mycorrhizal fungi.

checks.recorded: "dig a hole roughly twice the width of the plant's roots and the depth of a spade's blade."
checks.page_wording: For each rose dig a hole roughly twice the width of the plant's roots and the depth of a spade's blade.
checks.note: Word for word, in 'How to plant roses', and applies to each rose whether bare-root or potted. It is one data point for 'wider than the roots'.

checks.recorded: "is at soil level (not below as this is reported to increase the risk of rose dieback)."
checks.page_wording: ensure the graft union (...) is at soil level (not below as this is reported to increase the risk of rose dieback).
checks.note: Word for word. The instruction is given for 'each rose' in the planting steps and puts the graft union at soil level, which is one of the three positions the finding lists.

checks.recorded: "is at soil level (not below as this is reported to increase the risk of rose dieback)."
checks.page_wording: ensure the graft union (...) is at soil level (not below as this is reported to increase the risk of rose dieback).
checks.note: Word for word, and it supports the RHS half: not below soil level, with the reason given as 'reported to increase the risk of rose dieback' (reported, not stated as fact). This page says nothing about cold winters or frost in connection with union depth, so that half rests on other sources.

checks.recorded: "Prune back in the first winter after planting. Do this in late winter or early spring."
checks.page_wording: Prune back in the first winter after planting. Do this in late winter or early spring.
checks.note: Word for word, under Aftercare, Pruning. As a data point: the RHS times pruning for the first winter after planting, not at planting, with amounts by type (hybrid teas 10-15 cm, floribundas about 15 cm, climbers and ramblers 30-40 cm 'if not already pruned at the nursery', shrub roses left unpruned). The page gives no instruction to prune at planting.

checks.recorded: Consistency (BASICCARE F2): "Water well in dry spells for at least two summers after planting."
checks.page_wording: Water well in dry spells for at least two summers after planting.
checks.note: Word for word, under Aftercare, general care.

contradictions: Bare-root timing is qualified: 'Avoid planting in the middle of winter when the ground is frozen', and the page gives two windows (late autumn at leaf fall; late winter to early spring), which is narrower than a plain 'late autumn to early spring' (AF-1, AF-3).
The page gives no spacing distances, so it cannot support the 50 cm to 1 m range in AF-9.
The page calls replant disease 'soil sickness' and does not describe its effects (AF-11).
Within the RHS the soil-swap size differs: 45 cm depth and width here, about 60 cm across and at least 30 cm deep on the RHS replant disease page (AF-13).

checks.recorded: "New plantings may struggle to establish, make poor growth and may even die"
checks.page_wording: New plantings may struggle to establish, make poor growth and may even die.
checks.note: Word for word, in the list introduced by 'Plants affected by replant disease may show the following'. The page says 'Roses are particularly prone, though it can affect other trees and shrubs' and uses both 'replant disorder or replant disease' and 'rose sickness'.

checks.recorded: "Replant disease is a recognised but poorly understood problem."
checks.page_wording: Replant disease is a recognised but poorly understood problem.
checks.note: Word for word, and it is the only sentence on the page saying the problem is not understood. The page does offer a leading theory, worded as belief: 'It is believed to be caused by a build-up of soil pests and pathogens', with fungal root diseases and nematodes as 'favourite suspects' and soil sterilisation as evidence for a biological cause. So 'not established' holds, but 'unknown' would overstate it; the statement is about replant disease generally, not only roses.

checks.recorded: "This is usually about 60cm (2ft) diameter and at least 30cm (1ft) deep."
checks.page_wording: This is usually about 60cm (2ft) diameter and at least 30cm (1ft) deep.
checks.note: Word for word (one tool answer labelled it NEAR but gave identical wording). 'This' is the planting hole: the preceding lines are 'STEP 1: Swap the soil with fresh soil from another part of the garden' and that the hole should be a few centimetres larger than the root spread. The page also gives replanting on another site, a cardboard box lining, nitrogen feed, mycorrhizal products and organic matter in the backfill, and tolerant rootstocks; it does not mention rotating with other plants.

checks.recorded: "The problem can persist for at least nine years following removal of the first planting."
checks.page_wording: The problem can persist for at least nine years following removal of the first planting.
checks.note: Word for word. It sits in the explanation of the pest-and-pathogen theory and is about replant disease in general, not roses in particular. No source or study is cited on the page for the nine years.

contradictions: The page gives a leading explanation (build-up of soil pests and pathogens; sterilisation removes the problem, 'suggesting a biological cause'), which qualifies a bare statement that the cause is not established (AF-12).
The page does not mention crop rotation or growing other plants first, so it does not support the 'rotate with other plants' remedy in AF-13.
The page lists remedies not named in AF-13: lining the hole with a cardboard box, high-nitrogen fertiliser, and tolerant rootstocks such as Rosa 'Laxa'.
The nine-year statement is general to replant disease, not specific to roses (AF-14).

checks.recorded: "Move at any time during the dormant season from late October to mid-March"
checks.page_wording: Deciduous plants: Move at any time during the dormant season from late October to mid-March
checks.note: Word for word, under 'Timing', which opens 'The optimum time to move established trees or shrubs depends on their type'. It is general guidance for deciduous trees and shrubs, not written about roses, though the page names Rosa elsewhere. Evergreens are treated differently ('Best moved during October or late March').

checks.recorded: "Thin the growth lightly by pruning out any old, worn-out wood, but do not prune hard."
checks.page_wording: Thin the growth lightly by pruning out any old, worn-out wood, but do not prune hard.
checks.note: Word for word, but the context is narrower than the finding suggests: it is the third step under 'Preparation', which begins 'If possible prepare mature specimens a year in advance', after digging a root-pruning trench in November to February. It supports 'do not prune hard', for mature trees and shrubs generally, as year-ahead preparation; the 'Lifting and moving' steps themselves mention no pruning. Two tool answers disagreed on the neighbouring sentence; a third pass settled it as: before, 'Back fill the trench with sharp sand...'; after, 'Where necessary, re-shaping can be done once the plant is well re-established'.

checks.recorded: "Ensure that plants are watered in thoroughly after planting and during dry spells"
checks.page_wording: Ensure that plants are watered in thoroughly after planting and during dry spells
checks.note: Word for word, a bullet under 'Aftercare', whose opening sentence sets the period as the year after moving. General to moved trees and shrubs, not rose-specific. The page words the duration as a year, not 'until it recovers'; it also advises a thick mulch.

checks.recorded: "Plants resenting root disturbance such as Rosa, Magnolia, Cytisus and Cistus can be tricky to move." / "plants that have been growing in position for more than five years are much less likely to survive transplanting"
checks.page_wording: Plants resenting root disturbance such as Rosa... can be tricky to move. / ...plants... more than five years are much less likely to survive transplanting...
checks.note: Both fragments are word for word. The five-year rule of thumb applies to trees and shrubs generally and the page gives no age limit for roses, as the finding says. Note that the Rosa sentence says roses are tricky to move because they resent root disturbance, at any age, not only when old.

contradictions: The 'do not prune hard' advice is part of preparing mature specimens a year in advance, not an instruction for the day of the move (AF-29).
The page says Rosa resents root disturbance and 'can be tricky to move' whatever its age, which is a stronger caution than 'older roses are harder to move' (AF-34).
The dormant-season window is stated for deciduous plants only; evergreens are 'Best moved during October or late March' (AF-26).

checks.recorded: "it is likely that they are suffering from a problem known as replant disorder or rose sickness."
checks.page_wording: If you planted your new roses straight into soil where other roses had recently been grown then it is likely... replant disorder or rose sickness.
checks.note: Word for word, in the 'Roots' section, answering a question about new roses that never thrived in an old rose border. The next sentence gives the effects: 'This is characterised by poor establishment, dieback and a lack of healthy fine, feeder roots.' The answer says 'replant disorder or rose sickness' (not 'replant disease'), is worded as 'likely', and gives no remedy.

checks.recorded: "Bare rooted plants are dormant – they have no leaves or flowers and are only available in winter."
checks.page_wording: Bare rooted plants are dormant – they have no leaves or flowers and are only available in winter.
checks.note: Word for word. It says bare-root roses are dormant and are sold only in winter; it does not say when to plant them, and the page gives no planting months. Planting in winter is implied, not stated, and it covers Australia (New South Wales) only.

checks.recorded: "It is best to soak bare rooted roses in a bucket of water for 24 hours before planting in the garden."
checks.page_wording: It is best to soak bare rooted roses in a bucket of water for 24 hours before planting in the garden.
checks.note: Word for word. Plain recommendation to soak before planting.

checks.recorded: "soak bare rooted roses in a bucket of water for 24 hours"
checks.page_wording: It is best to soak bare rooted roses in a bucket of water for 24 hours before planting in the garden.
checks.note: Word for word, and it supplies the 24-hour end of the range. Here 24 hours is the recommended soak ('It is best'), not a limit or maximum. The same society's care calendar says 'at least two hours'.

contradictions: The page does not state a planting season for bare-root roses, only that they are available in winter (AF-1).
The page says bare-root roses can be stored in their transport packaging 'providing the roots are kept moist, for up to 14 days'.
The same society's care calendar gives a different soaking time ('at least two hours') from the 24 hours given here (AF-18).

checks.recorded: "Prepare the soil for planting in June/July."
checks.page_wording: Prepare the soil for planting in June/July.
checks.note: Word for word, under the 'Late April / May' heading, so it means prepare the soil now for planting in June/July. Bare-root planting steps then appear under June; the July section says nothing about planting. It supports the 'June to July' option for Australia only: May is not named as a planting month and the page says nothing about New Zealand. One tool answer misread the sentence as soil preparation in June/July; the heading it sits under rules that out.

checks.recorded: "Make a mound in the hole and place the roots over and down around the mound."
checks.page_wording: Make a mound in the hole and place the roots over and down around the mound.
checks.note: Word for word, under June (one tool answer cut the sentence short; a second confirmed the ending 'the mound'). About planting bare-root roses.

checks.recorded: "Before planting bare root roses soak the plants in a bucket of water with seaweed solution for at least two hours."
checks.page_wording: Before planting bare root roses soak the plants in a bucket of water with seaweed solution for at least two hours.
checks.note: Word for word, under June. Note the soak is in water with seaweed solution.

checks.recorded: "for at least two hours."
checks.page_wording: ...soak the plants in a bucket of water with seaweed solution for at least two hours.
checks.note: Word for word. Two hours is a minimum here ('at least') and no maximum is given; it falls inside the stated one-to-24-hour range.

checks.recorded: "sitting 3-5cm above ground level."
checks.page_wording: The bud union needs to be facing north or west and sitting 3-5cm above ground level.
checks.note: The fragment is word for word within this sentence, under June, and it is the bud union that sits above ground. It is the 'above the soil' data point. Written for New South Wales.

checks.recorded: "sitting 3-5cm above ground level."
checks.page_wording: The bud union needs to be facing north or west and sitting 3-5cm above ground level.
checks.note: Word for word. Supports the Australian part (bud union above ground level); nothing here about New Zealand.

checks.recorded: "Water well, poking around the roots to maintain soil and root contact."
checks.page_wording: Water well, poking around the roots to maintain soil and root contact.
checks.note: Word for word, under June. It comes straight after 'Backfill the soil halfway up the hole', so it describes watering part-way through backfilling, which is consistent with watering in thoroughly.

contradictions: The page names June/July, and only June carries planting steps; it does not name May as a planting month (AF-2).
Soaking time here ('at least two hours', with seaweed solution) differs from the 24 hours on the same society's Rose Growing Advice page (AF-18).
The page says nothing about trimming damaged roots or pruning at planting.

checks.recorded: "Bare root shrubs must be planted in spring before growth begins."
checks.page_wording: Bare root shrubs must be planted in spring before growth begins.
checks.note: Word for word, in the opening section; a later line reads 'Plant bare root shrubs, including roses, as soon as possible before spring growth begins', so roses are covered. Iowa is a cold-winter state. The page says 'must', which is stronger than 'prefer', and does not mention autumn planting.

checks.recorded: "store them in a cool, non-freezing location at around 40°F, such as a refrigerator"
checks.page_wording: If planting has to be delayed, store them in a cool, non-freezing location at around 40°F, such as a refrigerator, unheated garage, or root cellar.
checks.note: The fragment is word for word but is the exception for delayed planting, so on its own it shows only that roots are kept cool until planting. The same page carries direct support that was not recorded: 'Plant bare root shrubs as soon as possible after receiving them' and 'Do not let any part of the bare root shrub dry out, especially the root system.' Those sentences were reported in one tool answer and should be used instead.

checks.recorded: "dig a hole that is two to two-and-a-half times wider than the spread of the shrub's root system"
checks.page_wording: ...dig a hole that is two to two-and-a-half times wider than the spread of the shrub's root system.
checks.note: Word for word. One data point for a hole wider than the roots; written for bare-root shrubs including roses.

checks.recorded: "soak the shrubs' roots in a bucket of water for one to two hours"
checks.page_wording: Prior to planting, soak the shrubs' roots in a bucket of water for one to two hours.
checks.note: Word for word.

checks.recorded: "for one to two hours"
checks.page_wording: Prior to planting, soak the shrubs' roots in a bucket of water for one to two hours.
checks.note: Word for word, and it supplies the one-hour end of the range. This page gives no maximum soaking time, so it is not one of the two sources setting a 24-hour limit.

checks.recorded: "prune off damaged or broken roots"
checks.page_wording: Also, prune off damaged or broken roots.
checks.note: Word for word apart from the leading 'Also,'. It follows the soaking sentence and applies before planting.

checks.recorded: "the bud/graft union should be planted 2 to 4 inches below the soil surface"
checks.page_wording: In Iowa, the bud/graft union (denoted by a knob or crook in the plant stem) should be planted 2 to 4 inches below the soil...
checks.note: The recorded quotation drops the bracketed words '(denoted by a knob or crook in the plant stem)' without marking the gap, and drops the opening 'In Iowa,'. The meaning is unchanged: union 2 to 4 inches below the soil. The advice is explicitly for Iowa.

checks.recorded: "the bud/graft union should be planted 2 to 4 inches below the soil surface"
checks.page_wording: In Iowa, the bud/graft union (denoted by a knob or crook in the plant stem) should be planted 2 to 4 inches below the soil...
checks.note: Same unmarked omission as above. The cold-winter link is on the page but not in the recorded fragment: the sentence starts 'In Iowa,' and the next sentence is 'This helps protect the rose from harsh winter weather.' That following sentence should be recorded too. The RHS half rests on the RHS page.

checks.recorded: "Finally, water the shrub thoroughly."
checks.page_wording: Finally, water the shrub thoroughly.
checks.note: Word for word, the last planting step.

contradictions: The page says bare-root shrubs 'must' be planted in spring, a firmer statement than 'prefer spring' (AF-3).
The page gives no maximum soaking time; it should not be counted among sources that set 24 hours as a limit (AF-18).
The buried-union advice is limited to Iowa by the words 'In Iowa' (AF-20, AF-22).

checks.recorded: "The ideal moment is during dormancy, from late autumn to early spring."
checks.page_wording: The ideal moment is during dormancy, from late autumn to early spring.
checks.note: Word for word. The sentence names no country or months; the page is on the UK site of a UK nursery. Supports the UK part only.

checks.recorded: "keep the roses in their packaging in a cool, dry place, protected from frost, for up to three weeks."
checks.page_wording: If planting will be delayed, keep the roses in their packaging in a cool, dry place, protected from frost, for up to three weeks.
checks.note: The fragment is word for word, but it says the opposite of prompt planting: roses may be kept in their packaging for up to three weeks if planting is delayed. Two passes found no wording such as 'as soon as possible' or 'on arrival' and no instruction to keep roots from drying out; the only related line is the pre-planting soak 'to rehydrate them'.

checks.recorded: "Select a location that enjoys at least four hours of direct sun each day."
checks.page_wording: Select a location that enjoys at least four hours of direct sun each day.
checks.note: Word for word. It is the four-hour end of the stated range. Commercial source, dated 29 September 2025.

checks.recorded: "Before planting, soak the roots in water for a couple of hours to rehydrate them."
checks.page_wording: Before planting, soak the roots in water for a couple of hours to rehydrate them.
checks.note: Word for word.

checks.recorded: "soak the roots in water for a couple of hours"
checks.page_wording: Before planting, soak the roots in water for a couple of hours to rehydrate them.
checks.note: Word for word. 'A couple of hours' sits inside the one-to-24-hour range; no maximum is given.

checks.recorded: "keeping the graft union 2-3 inches, 5-8 cm, below the soil surface"
checks.page_wording: Plant the rose as you would in the ground, keeping the graft union 2-3 inches, 5-8 cm, below the soil surface.
checks.note: The fragment is word for word but appears only under 'Shrub Roses in a Pot' and 'Climbing Roses in a Pot'. This page gives no in-ground planting steps or depth; it links to separate guides for that. The words 'as you would in the ground' suggest the same depth applies in the garden, but the page does not say so directly and gives no reason for the depth.

checks.recorded: "Water deeply after planting so the soil settles around the roots."
checks.page_wording: Water deeply after planting so the soil settles around the roots.
checks.note: Word for word, under 'Caring for Newly Planted Roses', which is not limited to pots or to the ground.

contradictions: The page allows bare-root roses to be held in their packaging for up to three weeks, in a 'cool, dry place', and does not say to plant promptly or to keep roots moist; this qualifies AF-5.
The below-soil graft union depth is stated only in the pot-planting sections of this page (AF-20).
The page gives no reason for burying the graft union, and no link to cold winters (relevant to AF-22 if this source is relied on there).

checks.recorded: "The best time to transplant is always during the dormant season in early spring"
checks.page_wording: The best time to transplant is always during the dormant season in early spring as it will cause less stress and shock to the plant.
checks.note: Word for word. Note the page narrows dormancy to 'early spring' and does not mention late autumn or winter. US own-root rose nursery, dated 13 April 2023.

checks.recorded: "roses are adaptable to being moved to a new home"
checks.page_wording: Well, it's a good thing that roses are adaptable to being moved to a new home!
checks.note: The fragment is word for word, but it is about choosing a new spot (the next lines say roses like 'brand new homes'), not about the time of year. The page does support the finding in a different passage that was not recorded: the section 'Transplanting During the Growing Season' opens 'If you need to transplant your rose during the growing season (non-dormant), you can still be successful but water is key!' That section stresses watering (water deeply beforehand, vitamin B1 feed) but its pruning step is not heavier than the dormant one.

checks.recorded: "Cut the rose canes back to 10-12 inches and remove any foliage"
checks.page_wording: Cut the rose canes back to 10-12 inches and remove any foliage so the plant can focus on root development in its new home.
checks.note: Word for word, as a step under 'Transplanting While Dormant'. One data point for cutting back before moving. The growing-season section words it differently: prune out dried or dead material and 'cut the taller canes down to a manageable height before digging up the rose'.

checks.recorded: "Take as many of the roots with you as possible."
checks.page_wording: Take as many of the roots with you as possible and gently transfer to the new hole.
checks.note: Word for word, in both the dormant and growing-season sections. It supports keeping as many roots as possible. The page gives no root-ball size and says nothing about keeping soil on the roots; the nearest line is 'Remove the rose by digging far enough away from the root ball so you don't damage the roots.'

checks.recorded: "Water the new rose every day for a week or two depending on your weather."
checks.page_wording: Water the new rose every day for a week or two depending on your weather.
checks.note: Word for word, in both sections. It supports watering and continued watering, but for a fixed 'week or two', not 'until it recovers', and nothing is said about watering after that. The page adds 'Do not fertilize or use any insecticides until you see new growth on the rose.'

contradictions: The quotation recorded for AF-27 is about choosing a new location, not about moving outside dormancy; the supporting text is the section 'Transplanting During the Growing Season'.

For growing-season moves the page asks for more watering ('water is key') but not clearly more pruning: the dormant step is the more specific cut (10-12 inches), which qualifies the 'more pruning' part of AF-27.
The page puts the best time 'in early spring' only, narrower than 'while dormant' (AF-26).
The page does not mention keeping soil on the roots or a root-ball size (AF-30).

checks.recorded: "Roses can be used in many situations but do best in full sun."
checks.page_wording: Roses can be used in many situations but do best in full sun.
checks.note: Word for word. It supports a sunny site ('do best in full sun') but the page states no number of hours, so it does not support the four-to-six-hour range.

checks.recorded: "They should be sheltered from strong winds and have good drainage."
checks.page_wording: They should be sheltered from strong winds and have good drainage.
checks.note: Word for word. It supports the need for good drainage. The page does not mention raised beds or mounds; for heavy soils it says 'add compost before planting and gypsum to particularly heavy soils, like clay'.

checks.recorded: "Always plant at the same depth as they are in their container."
checks.page_wording: Always plant at the same depth as they are in their container.
checks.note: Word for word, in the planting section of a page about roses, following 'Planting is best done in autumn or winter.' The page refers only to container plants and never mentions bare-root roses or the bud union. New Zealand (Auckland) source.

contradictions: For heavy soil the page recommends compost and gypsum, not raised beds or mounds (AF-7).
The page says 'Planting is best done in autumn or winter', which qualifies any claim that potted roses can be planted through most of the year (AF-4, if this source is used there).
No hours of sun are stated (AF-6).

sources.page_date: not shown (PDF sits in a 2015/10 upload folder; no date in the document)

checks.recorded: "This is best done in June or July."
checks.page_wording: Planting winter bare rooted roses: This is best done in June or July.
checks.note: Sits directly under the heading 'Planting winter bare rooted roses', so it supports winter bare-root planting in (South) Australia. The page does not say the roses are planted 'while dormant' (the word appears only about dormant buds and suckers), and it says nothing about the UK or New Zealand.

checks.recorded: "This is best done in June or July."
checks.page_wording: Planting winter bare rooted roses: This is best done in June or July.
checks.note: Supports the 'June to July' option for an Australian source, for bare-rooted roses. May is not mentioned on this page; the New Zealand half of the finding is not something this source can support.

checks.recorded: "Roses like full sun with at least 5 to 6 hours of direct sunlight each day."
checks.page_wording: Roses like full sun with at least 5 to 6 hours of direct sunlight each day.
checks.note: Under 'The Rose Bed'. Gives a minimum of 5 to 6 hours of direct sun, which is inside the four-to-six-hour range the finding states.

checks.recorded: "Soil must be well drained, preferably neutral and containing copious quantities of organic matter."
checks.page_wording: Soil must be well drained, preferably neutral and containing copious quantities of organic matter.
checks.note: Supports the well-drained soil part. The page does not mention raised beds or mounds; for alkaline clay soil it says to work in gypsum, compost, fertiliser and/or mulch.

checks.recorded: "Avoid root competition from nearby trees and shrubs."
checks.page_wording: Avoid root competition from nearby trees and shrubs.
checks.note: Word for word, in the rose bed/site advice. Supports the finding in full.

checks.recorded: "The new rose will not tolerate any old rose roots remaining in its root zone."
checks.page_wording: Often called 'rose sick soil', the new rose will not tolerate any old rose roots remaining in its root zone.
checks.note: The recorded words are the second half of a sentence that begins "Often called 'rose sick soil'". The next sentence says the new rose 'will not die, but will not thrive for many months'. The page's term is 'rose sick soil', not 'replant disease' or 'rose sickness'; section is about replacing a single old rose.

checks.recorded: "Remove the old plant with as many roots as possible, plus an extra 2 buckets of soil."
checks.page_wording: Remove the old plant with as many roots as possible, plus an extra 2 buckets of soil.
checks.note: Followed by 'Replace with fresh garden soil from an area free of roses.' Supports soil replacement as this source's remedy, with a stated amount (2 buckets). It does not mention the other remedies (rotation, compost, mycorrhizal fungi).

checks.recorded: "Dig a hole 30cm square by a spade depth."
checks.page_wording: Dig a hole 30cm square by a spade depth.
checks.note: Gives a stated hole size for a bare-rooted rose, so it supports 'stated sizes vary'. The page does not say the hole should be wider than the roots.

checks.recorded: "Position the roots over the soil mound"

checks.recorded: "It is very important to keep the roots moist until planting into the new location."
checks.page_wording: It is very important to keep the roots moist until planting into the new location. Never let the roots dry out.
checks.note: Word for word, under 'Dormant Transplanting'; the roots go into a bucket of plain water for the move. This page does not mention watering the day before (the finding attributes that to one other source).

checks.recorded: "if kept moist it will recover."

checks.note: Fragment is word for word, but it is under 'Transplanting during the growing season'. checks.recorded: "The older the rose, the more likely that it will not appreciate being moved, although it is possible." / "If your plant has been settled for many years it does become tricky."
checks.page_wording: The older the rose, the more likely that it will not appreciate being moved, although it is possible. / ...it does become tricky.
checks.note: Both sentences are word for word, in the introduction. The page gives no age limit in years, which matches the finding.

contradictions: For dormant moves the page says to shake the soil from the roots, carry the rose in a bucket of water and replant it as a bare-root rose; this conflicts with 'keeping as much soil as possible' (AF-30) except for growing-season moves.
'Prune to at least half' is for growing-season moves only, not for winter moves.

checks.recorded: "a minimum of six hours of direct sunlight is recommended."
checks.page_wording: For best results, a minimum of six hours of direct sunlight is recommended.
checks.note: Fragment is word for word; preceded by 'Roses thrive on direct sunlight.' Gives the six-hour end of the range, as a recommendation 'for best results'.

checks.recorded: "60-100cm from other roses (depending on the size of the rose at maturity)."
checks.page_wording: Plant your rose 100cm away from other plants and 60-100cm from other roses (depending on the size of the rose at maturity).
checks.note: Fragment is word for word, under 'Avoid intense competition from other plants'. 60-100 cm sits inside 50 cm-1 m and depends on mature size. The guide covers several rose types and does not limit this figure to bush roses; the reason given is competition for moisture and sunlight.

checks.recorded: "Soak it well for 24 hours in a bucket of cold water before planting into the ground."
checks.page_wording: Soak it well for 24 hours in a bucket of cold water before planting into the ground.
checks.note: Word for word in two of three readings (a third shortened it), under 'Planting a bareroot rose', after 'Plant your bareroot rose as soon as possible.'

checks.recorded: "Soak it well for 24 hours in a bucket of cold water"
checks.page_wording: Soak it well for 24 hours in a bucket of cold water before planting into the ground.
checks.note: Gives the 24-hour top of the range. It is an instruction to soak for 24 hours, not a statement that 24 hours is a limit, and it is a New Zealand commercial source, not a US extension one.

checks.recorded: "Ensure you plant the rose up to the crown where all the shoots/branches are coming out from."
checks.page_wording: Ensure you plant the rose up to the crown where all the shoots/branches are coming out from.
checks.note: Word for word (it appears under both the potted and bareroot headings). The page never uses 'bud union' or 'graft'; it speaks of the 'crown'. A caption says 'This is the correct depth - the crown is sitting at soil level, unless you are planting a Standard (Tree) Rose.' So it supports 'at soil level' only if crown is read as bud union, and the page adds that a long shank 'needs to be well buried'.

contradictions: Uses 'crown', not 'bud union'; the depth rule excludes standard (tree) roses.
'Some of the budded roses have a long shank between the roots and crown. The shank needs to be well buried...' - a deep-planting instruction for the shank.
Spacing reason is competition for moisture and sunlight, not air circulation.

checks.recorded: "The old method of dealing with rose replant disease was to remove all the old soil and replace it with fresh soil."
checks.page_wording: The old method of dealing with rose replant disease was to remove all the old soil and replace it with fresh soil.
checks.note: Word for word, but this sentence only names 'rose replant disease' and an old remedy. The poor-growth claim is elsewhere and reported second-hand: 'The reasons cited are because the new roses won't do well and may even die', followed by 'There are mixed feelings about this with some people saying it's true and some saying it isn't.' The term 'rose sickness' is not used.

checks.recorded: "It has been proven that roses treated with mycorrhizal fungi thrive in soil where roses used to be."
checks.page_wording: It has been proven that roses treated with mycorrhizal fungi thrive in soil where roses used to be.
checks.note: Word for word. The article supplies two of the remedies: mycorrhizal fungi and adding well-rotted manure or compost, and mentions soil replacement as the 'old method'. The 'has been proven' claim has no source or study cited, and it does not mention rotation, planting elsewhere or how much soil to replace.

contradictions: The article presents replant disease as disputed: 'some people saying it's true and some saying it isn't'.
'It has been proven' is unsupported by any citation on the page; a reader comment asks for the studies.
Author treats soil replacement as outdated ('Luckily there is a much easier method').
Byline shows an email address (lbergeron@taunton.com); the article is signed 'Paul'.

checks.recorded: "plant them anywhere from 20 inches to 30 inches apart depending on the ultimate size of the plant."
checks.page_wording: ...I choose good Garden Roses and plant them anywhere from 20 inches to 30 inches apart depending on the ultimate size of the plant.
checks.note: Fragment is word for word; 20-30 inches is about 51-76 cm, inside the range, and it depends on ultimate size. But it is the author's own deliberately close planting of disease-resistant 'Garden Roses' for a carpet of bloom, set against rose guides that say to space far apart. Bush roses are not named, no metric figure is given, and he adds that warmer climates may need wider spacing.

checks.recorded: "The reason given is that magic air circulation argument."
checks.page_wording: The reason given is that magic air circulation argument. Air circulation is supposed to prevent disease.
checks.note: Word for word. The author goes on to question it: 'To which my response always is, why are you planting disease prone roses in the first place!' This is the source that questions the air-circulation reason.

contradictions: The 20-30 inch figure is closer than the rose guides the author is arguing against, which he says recommend spacing roses 'far apart so they don't touch each other'.
Climate qualifier: 'If you live in warmer climates you may need to space them further apart. Cooler climates can go tighter'.

checks.recorded: Plant bare root shrubs as soon as possible after receiving them
checks.page_wording: Plant bare root shrubs as soon as possible after receiving them.
checks.note: Word for word, under the heading "Care Before Planting". It is written about bare-root shrubs generally (the page title covers shrubs and roses), about planting, not moving. It carries only the "planted promptly" half of AF-5; the drying-out half is in the next recorded sentence. If planting is delayed the page allows cool storage at about 40F with damp packing.

checks.recorded: Do not let any part of the bare root shrub dry out, especially the root system.
checks.page_wording: Do not let any part of the bare root shrub dry out, especially the root system.
checks.note: Word for word, under "Care Before Planting", about bare-root shrubs generally (roses included by the page title). It carries only the "roots not allowed to dry out" half of AF-5; taken with the previous sentence the page supports the whole finding.

checks.recorded: This helps protect the rose from harsh winter weather.
checks.page_wording: This helps protect the rose from harsh winter weather.
checks.note: Word for word, under "Planting". "This" refers to the sentence before it: "In Iowa, the bud/graft union ... should be planted 2 to 4 inches below the soil surface", for grafted roses (hybrid tea, grandiflora, floribunda). Supports the first half of AF-22 (burying linked to cold winters, Iowa). The RHS/dieback half is not on this page at all.

contradictions: The page permits delayed planting: store bare-root plants at around 40F with the packing kept damp but not wet, so "as soon as possible" is not absolute.

checks.recorded: If you need to transplant your rose during the growing season (non-dormant), you can still be successful but water is key!
checks.page_wording: If you need to transplant your rose during the growing season (non-dormant), you can still be successful but water is key!
checks.note: Word for word, under the heading "Transplanting During the Growing Season"; about moving an established rose while in growth. The section goes on to say water deeply beforehand, cut taller canes "down to a manageable height", and "Water the new rose every day for a week or two depending on your weather". The seller is an own-root rose nursery (US).

contradictions: Pruning is optional on this page: "You can also choose not to cut the rose back, and it will show you how much it can support by wilting at the tips."

checks.recorded: Aim to preserve as much of the root system as possible.
checks.page_wording: Aim to preserve as much of the root system as possible.
checks.note: Word for word, under "Step 3: Lift the Rose"; about lifting an established rose to move it. It supports keeping as many roots as possible. It does not say to keep soil on the roots or to dig as large a root ball as practicable; the only size given is "Begin digging at least a spade's width from the base".

checks.recorded: the graft union should sit around 2 inches below soil level
checks.page_wording: The graft union, the swollen area where the rose has been grafted onto its rootstock, should sit around 2 inches below soil level.
checks.note: The recorded words are exact but are the two ends of a longer sentence with a clause in between. It sits under "Step 4: Replant with Care", so it is about replanting a moved rose, not first planting. It supplies the "below soil level" position (about 2 inches; inches only, no cm) for AF-20, which is as far as one source can go on a "sources differ" finding.

checks.recorded: can still be done, but you may see some temporary signs of stress
checks.page_wording: If you need to move a rose during the growing season, it can still be done, but you may see some temporary signs...
checks.note: Recorded fragment is word for word, under "When is the Best Time to Move a Rose?". The next sentences add: "Keep the rose well-watered and consider using liquid seaweed to support it while it settles." So it supports moving outside dormancy with more watering; the page asks for no extra pruning for a growing-season move. Best time stated is November to February (UK and Europe).

checks.recorded: (what does the page tell the gardener to do if a rose has grown in the new spot before? quote it)
checks.page_wording: "Remove as much of the soil from the previous planting hole as reasonably possible and replace it with fresh soil" / "Adding well-rotted manure or soil improver will help"
checks.note: The page answers the question under the heading "What if a Rose Has Grown There Before?": "If the new position has previously been home to another rose, there is one additional step to take before planting", then replace the soil (fresh soil from elsewhere in the garden or good-quality topsoil) and add well-rotted manure or soil improver. No measured amount of soil is given. The reader also reported a sub-heading "Replant with Mycorrhizal Fungi" in that section in three of four answers, with no text under it, and one listing of headings did not show it; treat the mycorrhizal part as unconfirmed. The page does not use the words "replant disease" or "rose sickness".

contradictions: The page advises pruning before moving ("Step 2: Prune Before Moving": cut back some top growth), and does not tell the gardener to keep soil on the roots.
Graft-union depth of about 2 inches below soil is given for replanting a moved rose; it conflicts with sources that put the union at or above soil level (which is the point of AF-20).

further_sentences_confirmed.page_date: 9 November 2020 (author Ron Daniels, ARS Master Consulting Rosarian)

checks.recorded: taking care to damage as few of the roots as possible
checks.page_wording: Lift the root ball of the dormant plant ... with a shovel, taking care to damage as few of the roots as possible.
checks.note: Recorded fragment is word for word; it is about lifting a dormant established rose to move it (late winter to early spring; December to early February in zone 7, per the page). It supports keeping as many roots as possible. The page gives a fixed digging distance ("Carefully dig around the plant (18 to 24 inches) to cut roots on all sides") and says nothing about keeping soil on the roots or digging as large a ball as practicable.

contradictions: The page accepts root loss: "Cut the canes back by 1/2 to compensate for root loss." (given as a step at replanting).

checks.recorded: prune off any damaged or broken roots
checks.page_wording: Remove the rose plant from its packaging or pot, remove excess soil and prune off any damaged or broken roots.
checks.note: Recorded fragment is word for word. It is step 3 under "How to Grow Roses in a Garden" and the same wording appears again as step 3 under "How to Grow Roses in a Pot". "Packaging or pot" means it applies to both bare-root and potted roses at planting. New Zealand, commercial (garden products).

further_sentences_confirmed.page_date: Q&A entries individually dated; those checked are August 2007, January 2010 and November 2012 (page as a whole: no single date)

checks.recorded: If you must move them this fall, it can be done, but I would avoid pruning if possible
checks.page_wording: If you must move them this fall, it can be done, but I would avoid pruning if possible.
checks.note: Word for word, in the August 2007 entry about moving rose bushes within a yard (Arkansas). It supports "do not prune first" only for an autumn move; the reason given is "Pruned roses heading into fall and winter would make them more susceptible to winter damage." The same answer says the best time to move is February, "the same time we prune them", so it is not advice against pruning in general.

checks.recorded: for roses, I suggest moving them after you prune them in February
checks.page_wording: For roses, I suggest moving them after you prune them in February so you deal with less thorns.
checks.note: Recorded fragment is exact apart from the capital F and the dropped ending "so you deal with less thorns". January 2010 entry about moving several plants (roses, butterfly bush, herbs), Arkansas. It supports late winter and after pruning; the reason given is convenience (fewer thorns), not plant health, and the entry gives November to February as the general dormant window.

checks.recorded: Plant it in the ground, mulch it and water if dry and it should do well.
checks.page_wording: Yes, plant it in the ground, mulch it and water if dry and it should do well.
checks.note: Recorded wording is exact apart from the leading "Yes," and capital P. But the November 2012 entry is about planting out a pot-grown Knock Out rose raised from a cutting, not about moving an established rose, and "water if dry" is weaker than "watered well and kept watered until it recovers". It is thin support for AF-33. The August 2007 entry (about moved rose bushes) was reported to say "water well, and mulch" and "Monitor the plant this winter", which fits the finding better but was not the quotation recorded.

contradictions: September 2012 entry (as reported): "prune as little as possible to make the move feasible" and heavy autumn pruning makes roses more susceptible to winter damage; this qualifies "most sources cut back top growth before moving" for autumn moves.
All advice is for Arkansas (mild-winter southern US); February pruning and moving dates are regional.

further_sentences_confirmed.page_date: not shown (only related-article dates of 2021 appear)

checks.recorded: Firm the soil down gently and water in well with Aquaticus Organic Garden Booster.
checks.page_wording: Firm the soil down gently and water in well with Aquaticus Organic Garden Booster.
checks.note: Word for word, under the heading "Plant". The steps begin "Gently tap the plant out of its pot", so it is about planting a potted rose in the garden; the same sentence is repeated in the section on planting in containers. The watering-in is tied to a named product sold by the garden centre. Bare-root roses are not addressed in this section.

checks.recorded: Firm down and water thoroughly.
checks.page_wording: Firm down and water thoroughly.
checks.note: Word for word, under the heading "Container grown roses", which is about planting a nursery-pot rose into the garden ("Fill to top of hole. Firm down and water thoroughly."). The page does not mention bare-root roses at all, so support is for potted roses only. The page also says "Regular watering will be required to get plants established."

contradictions: The page says "Container grown roses can be planted in your garden at any time of the year" but also "The best planting time for all rose varieties is from winter through to spring" (not part of AF-24, but relevant to planting-time findings).

checks.recorded: Avoid planting in the middle of winter when the ground is frozen
checks.page_wording: Avoid planting in the middle of winter when the ground is frozen.
checks.note: Word for word, in the bare-root roses part of the page. On its own it is only the frozen-ground caveat. The UK timing in AF-1 is carried by the sentence before it: "Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes." The page says nothing about New Zealand or Australia, so that part of AF-1 is not supported here.

contradictions: The RHS wording gives two windows (late autumn at leaf fall; late winter to early spring) and tells the gardener to avoid midwinter when the ground is frozen, so "late autumn to early spring" as one unbroken season slightly overstates it.

checks.recorded: providing the roots are kept moist, for up to 14 days
checks.page_wording: ...can be stored in their transport packaging, providing the roots are kept moist, for up to 14 days.
checks.note: Recorded fragment is word for word; the full sentence begins "They are cheaper to buy than potted roses, are quick and easy to transport and". It is about storing bare-root roses before planting. It supports keeping the roots moist. It does not support "planted promptly": the page nowhere says as soon as possible, immediately or promptly, and instead allows up to 14 days in the packaging.

contradictions: Qualifies AF-5: bare-root roses "can be stored in their transport packaging ... for up to 14 days" if roots are kept moist; the page also says to soak them in water for 24 hours before planting.

further_sentences_confirmed.page_date: 9 April 2024 (author Loren Desbruslais; reader also reported "last modified 4 September 2025")

checks.recorded: Shrub roses are usually planted about 1m apart
checks.page_wording: Small or miniature rose varieties are often at their best in containers, while shrub roses are usually planted about 1m apart.
checks.note: The recorded words are on the page but as the second half of a longer sentence, not a sentence of their own (so lower-case "shrub"); it sits under "How to plant roses". One answer presented it as a separate sentence and a later answer quoting the whole paragraph showed it is a clause; I report the paragraph version. It supports only the 1 m upper figure, for "shrub roses". The page does not say spacing depends on mature size and gives no 50 cm spacing; its stated reason is air circulation, "especially in humid climates".

contradictions: The other distances on the page (40-50cm+ container diameter; hole 60cm wide and 30cm deep) are not plant spacings and must not be read as such.

checks.recorded: add compost before planting and gypsum to particularly heavy soils, like clay
checks.page_wording: In heavy soils add compost before planting and gypsum to particularly heavy soils, like clay.
checks.note: Recorded fragment is word for word; the sentence opens "In heavy soils", under "How to plant". The same section says roses "should be sheltered from strong winds and have good drainage", which supports the drainage half (the page does not use the words "well-drained"). The page does not mention raised beds or mounds; its remedy for heavy soil is compost and gypsum.

checks.recorded: Planting is best done in autumn or winter
checks.page_wording: Planting is best done in autumn or winter.
checks.note: Word for word, under "How to plant". It does not say container roses can be planted through most of the year; the page gives no other planting time and does not mention bare-root roses. The next sentence ("Always plant at the same depth as they are in their container") shows the advice is about container-grown plants, so the page narrows planting to autumn or winter and can serve AF-4 only as a qualifying condition, not as support.

contradictions: "Planting is best done in autumn or winter" (said of roses planted from containers) qualifies AF-4's "through most of the year".
For heavy soil the page recommends compost and gypsum, not raised beds or mounds (AF-7).

checks.recorded: Where temperatures don't drop below -10 degrees Fahrenheit, either fall or spring planting is satisfactory
checks.page_wording: Where temperatures don't drop below -10 degrees Fahrenheit, either fall or spring planting is satisfactory.
checks.note: Word for word, under the heading "Planting roses" (general planting time, not limited to bare-root). The recorded sentence itself says either season is satisfactory in milder areas; the cold-winter spring preference in AF-3 is in the next sentence, which was not recorded: "If you live in an area where winter temperatures dip below -10 degrees Fahrenheit, spring planting is preferred." The RHS half of AF-3 is not on this page.

checks.recorded: If they are too large for the hole, don't cut them off
checks.page_wording: If they are too large for the hole, don't cut them off.
checks.note: Word for word, under "Planting bare-root roses"; "they" are the roots, and the next sentence is "Replace the plant and dig a larger hole." This is advice NOT to cut healthy roots to fit the hole. The reader found no sentence on the page about trimming damaged or broken roots, so the quotation does not support AF-19; it is a qualifier (do not shorten sound roots). The reader gave two different versions of the sentence just before it ("Remove the plant from bucket or wrapping for prompt planting." and "Don't allow roots to dry."), so the exact preceding sentence is uncertain.

contradictions: AF-19: the page says not to cut off roots that are too large for the hole (dig a bigger hole instead) and has no instruction to trim damaged roots.
AF-3: in areas that do not fall below -10F the page treats fall and spring planting as equally satisfactory, so the spring preference applies only to the coldest areas.
Bud-union depth on this page varies by region: slightly below soil level in southeast Missouri, 2 inches below in northern Missouri.

further_sentences_confirmed.page_date: not shown for the answer; the book quoted is dated 1989

checks.recorded: Fill in with topsoil, make a ridge of soil around the base of the plant, and water well.
checks.page_wording: Fill in with topsoil, make a ridge of soil around the base of the plant, and water well.
checks.note: Word for word; about replanting an established rose that is being moved (from under a tree), with spring preferred and early spring or late fall both acceptable. The advice is quoted from "Roses: 1001 Gardening Questions Answered" (Garden Way Publishing, 1989), not the library's own. It supports watering well at replanting. For afterwards the page says only "Afterwards, water carefully, neither too much nor too little", with nothing about continuing until the rose recovers.

contradictions: After the initial watering the page counsels moderation ("neither too much nor too little"), which tempers "kept watered".
The page says to prune before moving, "leaving three to four canes", and to dig a trench one foot from the crown; it does not mention keeping a ball of soil.

checks.recorded: Keep as much soil around the roots as possible
checks.page_wording: When lifting the plant from the ground, make sure you keep as much soil around the roots as possible - the more the better.
checks.note: The recorded words are in this sentence (lower-case "keep"). One answer gave a shorter version of the sentence; when asked for it character for character the reader gave the wording shown. It sits under "Transplanting during the growing season" only. For a dormant (winter) move the same page says the opposite, so it supports AF-30 only for growing-season moves.

checks.recorded: (what does the page say to do with the soil on the roots when moving a rose in winter dormancy? quote it)
checks.page_wording: Reach down and pull the rose out by the base of the plant, giving it a shake to release the soil form the roots.
checks.note: The page answers the question under "Dormant Transplanting": the soil is shaken off ("form" is the page's typo for "from"), then "Place the rose roots into a bucket of plain water" and "You can then plant as a bare root rose in the new location." The digging circle is "about 45cm in diameter". This contradicts AF-30 for dormant moves: no soil is kept and the root ball is not maximised.

checks.recorded: Back fill the hole and water in well.
checks.page_wording: Back fill the hole and water in well.
checks.note: Word for word, once only, under "Transplanting during the growing season". The same section adds "Your plant may wilt a bit or just sit for a few weeks once in its new location but if kept moist it will recover", so the growing-season section supports the whole of AF-33. The "Dormant Transplanting" section, as read, has no sentence about watering after replanting, so support is limited to growing-season moves.

contradictions: AF-30: for winter-dormant moves the page says to shake the soil off the roots and replant as a bare-root rose; keeping soil applies only in the growing season.
For growing-season moves the page says "Prune to at least half of its size"; the dormant move is done after the winter prune.
